chem_ocra.13.2.summary: Catalysts are substances that increase the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or chemically changed at the end of the process. They work by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, meaning a greater proportion of colliding particles possess the minimum energy required to react successfully. Reaction profiles visually represent these energy changes, allowing us to compare catalysed and uncatalysed pathways for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.

core.p: A catalyst is a chemical substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction. Crucially, it remains chemically unchanged and unconsumed at the end of the reaction, meaning it can be recovered and reused indefinitely.
bullets: Increases the rate of reaction significantly
Remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction
Is not used up; mass at start equals mass at end
Does not alter the overall amount of products formed
Only a very small amount of catalyst is usually required

callouts.p: A substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction, without being used up or chemically changed by the end of the reaction.

core.p: Catalysts do not increase the collision frequency between reactant particles. Instead, they change the mechanism of the reaction entirely by providing an alternative reaction pathway that requires less energy.
bullets: Provides an alternative reaction pathway
Involves different steps or intermediates
Lowers the activation energy barrier
Does not change the energy of reactants or products
Does not change the overall enthalpy change (Delta H)

callouts.p: Catalysts work by lowering activation energy through an alternative pathway, not by increasing particle speed or collision frequency.

core.p: Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that particles must collide with in order for a chemical reaction to occur. By lowering this threshold, more collisions become successful.
bullets: Activation energy is abbreviated as Ea
Higher activation energy means fewer successful collisions
A catalyst lowers the activation energy (Ea)
A greater proportion of particles now have energy greater than or equal to the new lower Ea
Frequency of successful collisions increases, increasing the rate of reaction

callouts.p: The minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide in order for a chemical reaction to take place.

core.p: Reaction profiles are graphical representations that show how the energy of reactants and products changes during the course of a chemical reaction. They display energy on the vertical axis and progress of reaction on the horizontal axis.
bullets: Y-axis represents energy (kJ or kJ/mol)
X-axis represents progress of reaction or time
Reactants are plotted on the left-hand side
Products are plotted on the right-hand side
Peak represents the transition state or activation energy barrier

core.p: In an exothermic reaction, energy is released to the surroundings. The products have less energy than the reactants, resulting in a negative enthalpy change (Delta H).
bullets: Reactants start higher on the Y-axis than products
Overall energy change (Delta H) is negative
Curve rises to a peak representing activation energy from reactants
Curve falls below the reactant level to reach products
Surroundings warm up as energy is released

callouts.p: Products are lower in energy than reactants, showing energy has been released to the surroundings.

fig.cap: Reaction profile for an exothermic reaction showing the uncatalysed pathway and lower activation energy catalysed alternative pathway.

core.p: In an endothermic reaction, energy is absorbed from the surroundings. The products have more energy than the reactants, resulting in a positive enthalpy change (Delta H).
bullets: Reactants start lower on the Y-axis than products
Overall energy change (Delta H) is positive
Curve rises steeply to a high peak activation energy
Curve descends to products that sit higher than reactants
Surroundings cool down as energy is absorbed

callouts.p: Products are higher in energy than reactants, showing energy has been absorbed from the surroundings.

fig.cap: Reaction profile for an endothermic reaction, illustrating how the catalyst lowers the peak without changing reactant or product energy levels.

core.p: On a reaction profile diagram, the catalysed reaction path is shown by an alternative curve that has a lower maximum peak than the uncatalysed reaction path.
bullets: Uncatalysed path shown with a solid line and high peak
Catalysed path shown with a dashed or lower solid line
Peak for catalysed path is clearly lower than uncatalysed peak
Start point (reactants) and end point (products) remain identical
Distance from reactants to peak represents activation energy (Ea)

callouts.p: Always start and end the catalysed curve at the exact same heights as the uncatalysed curve. Only the peak height changes.

core.p: Activation energy is measured on a reaction profile as the vertical energy difference between the energy level of the reactants and the highest point (peak) of the curve.
bullets: Measure from reactant line up to the top of the curve peak
Uncatelysed Ea is the distance from reactants to the main peak
Catalysed Ea is the distance from reactants to the lower catalysed peak
Lower Ea value indicates faster reaction rate
Units are typically kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol)

core.h: Identifying Enthalpy Change (Delta H) on Profiles
core.p: The overall enthalpy change of a reaction is represented on a reaction profile by the vertical distance between the energy level of the reactants and the energy level of the products.
bullets: Measure from reactant line horizontally across to product level
Negative Delta H for exothermic (products lower than reactants)
Positive Delta H for endothermic (products higher than reactants)
Catalysts do not change Delta H
Do not confuse Delta H with activation energy

callouts.p: Students often mix up activation energy (reactants to peak) and enthalpy change (reactants to products). Check your definitions.

core.h: Types of Catalysts: Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous
core.p: Catalysts can be classified based on whether they are in the same physical state as the reactants or in a different state.
bullets: Homogeneous catalysts are in the same physical state as the reactants (e.g. all aqueous)
Heterogeneous catalysts are in a different physical state from the reactants (e.g. solid catalyst, gas reactants)
Transition metals and their compounds are excellent heterogeneous catalysts
Enzymes are complex biological homogeneous or heterogeneous catalysts in living systems
Heterogeneous catalysts often work by providing a surface for reactant molecules to adsorb onto

core.p: Catalysts are vital in industrial chemistry because they save money, reduce energy consumption, and increase production efficiency.
bullets: Allow reactions to take place at lower temperatures
Reduce energy demands and fuel costs for heating
Increase the rate of production per unit time
Can make previously uneconomical industrial processes viable
Examples include iron in the Haber process and platinum/rhodium in catalytic converters

callouts.p: Lower temperatures needed with catalysts mean less fossil fuels burned, reducing both costs and carbon footprint.

analogy.p: Imagine hikers trying to travel from one valley to another. Without a catalyst, they must climb right over the highest, steepest peak of the mountain range (the uncatalysed activation energy). A catalyst builds a tunnel straight through the lower part of the mountain (the alternative pathway with lower activation energy). Much less effort and energy is needed to cross, so many more hikers make the journey successfully in less time, while the mountain itself remains unchanged at the end. This breaks down because real reactant particles do not consciously choose routes; rather, the catalyst alters the chemical bonding pathways available.

terms.d: A substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or chemically changed.
The minimum amount of energy colliding particles must have to react.
A graph showing the energy changes during the course of a reaction from reactants to products.
A reaction that releases energy to the surroundings, resulting in products with less energy than reactants.
A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, resulting in products with more energy than reactants.
The overall change in thermal energy during a reaction, denoted as Delta H.
A different route for a chemical reaction that has a lower activation energy.
A catalyst that is in the same physical state as the reactants.
A catalyst that is in a different physical state from the reactants.
Elements from the central block of the periodic table, many of which act as effective catalysts.
A collision between particles that results in a reaction because particles have energy equal to or greater than activation energy.
The high-energy state corresponding to the peak of the activation energy barrier.

mistakes.w: A catalyst gets used up in the reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst is chemically unchanged and remains at the end of the reaction.

mistakes.w: A catalyst increases the total yield of a reaction.
mistakes.r: A catalyst only increases the rate of reaction; it does not change the amount of product formed.

mistakes.w: A catalyst provides energy to the particles.
mistakes.r: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, it does not add thermal energy.

mistakes.w: A catalyst changes the overall enthalpy change (Delta H).
mistakes.r: Delta H is determined solely by the energy of reactants and products, which remains unchanged by a catalyst.

mistakes.w: Activation energy is measured from the products to the peak.
mistakes.r: Activation energy is measured from the reactants to the peak.

mistakes.w: Catalysts increase the speed of reactant particles.
mistakes.r: Particle speed is determined by temperature, not catalysts. Catalysts lower activation energy.
Homogeneous catalysts are in the same state as reactants (e.g. aqueous or liquid), whereas solid catalysts are usually heterogeneous.

exam.q: Define what is meant by the term 'catalyst'.
model: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction
And is not used up / remains chemically unchanged at the end
exam.tip: Both marking points are essential for full marks.

exam.q: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction.
model: That has a lower activation energy
So a greater proportion of particles have energy exceeding the activation energy / more successful collisions
exam.tip: Mentioning lower activation energy and alternative pathway secures standard examiner points.

exam.q: State whether a catalyst changes the overall energy change (Delta H) of a reaction.
exam.tip: Keep direct answers short for 1-mark recall questions.

exam.q: Describe how activation energy is represented on a reaction profile diagram.
model: From the energy level of the reactants to the peak of the curve
exam.tip: Be precise with starting and ending points.

exam.q: A student draws a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction. On the same axes, draw and label the curve for the catalysed reaction.
model: Curve starts and ends at the exact same energy levels as the uncatalysed curve
Peak of the new curve is clearly lower than the original peak
exam.tip: Ensure your curve starts and finishes level with the original reactants and products.

exam.q: Explain why using a catalyst can reduce industrial heating costs.
model: Allowing reactions to be run at lower temperatures while maintaining rate
exam.tip: Link lower activation energy directly to reduced temperature and fuel usage.

exam.q: Distinguish between a homogeneous catalyst and a heterogeneous catalyst.
model: Homogeneous catalyst is in the same physical state as the reactants
Heterogeneous catalyst is in a different physical state from the reactants

exam.q: State one reason why transition metals are widely used as catalysts.
model: They make effective heterogeneous catalysts / they have variable oxidation states / they readily adsorb reactant molecules
exam.tip: Accept any valid property of transition metals acting as catalysts.

exam.q: Explain why adding a catalyst does not alter the amount of product formed in a batch reaction.
model: Catalysts only affect the rate of reaction
The amount of product is determined solely by the mass and moles of limiting reactants
exam.tip: Distinguish clearly between rate (how fast) and yield (how much).

worked.q: Use the reaction profile data to calculate the activation energy for the uncatalysed and catalysed reactions given: Reactants = 50 kJ/mol, Products = 20 kJ/mol, Uncatalysed peak = 130 kJ/mol, Catalysed peak = 90 kJ/mol.
steps: Identify the energy of the reactants: 50 kJ/mol.
Find the uncatalysed activation energy by subtracting reactant energy from the uncatalysed peak: 130 - 50 = 80 kJ/mol.
Find the catalysed activation energy by subtracting reactant energy from the catalysed peak: 90 - 50 = 40 kJ/mol.
worked.ans: Uncatalysed Ea = 80 kJ/mol; Catalysed Ea = 40 kJ/mol.

worked.q: Explain how the reaction profile for an endothermic reaction changes when a catalyst is added, referencing activation energy and enthalpy change.
steps: State that the reactant and product energy levels remain unchanged, so overall Delta H is unaffected.
Identify that the peak of the curve representing the activation energy is lower on the catalysed profile.
Conclude that the alternative pathway lowers the activation energy from reactants to the peak.
worked.ans: The reactant and product levels stay the same (positive Delta H unchanged), but the peak height is reduced, showing a lower activation energy.
